content: Several types of cancer and neurocognitive disorders have been associated with HIV, but initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) earlier has been shown to reduce these complications and improve survival rates. Evidence from a large randomized clinical trial demonstrates that ART significantly reduces sexual transmission of HIV to uninfected partners, not only in heterosexual serodiscordant couples but also among homosexual couples. The recommendation to start ART at any CD4 cell count is supported by a systematic review that evaluated evidence from one randomized controlled trial and 17 observational studies. These studies reported clinical, immunological, and virological outcomes, as well as HIV transmission rates. However, data from the START study, which was unpublished at the time of the guideline development, were not included in the systematic review due to differences in study design. The START trial findings, which were released early due to predefined stopping rules, showed a 57% reduction in adverse outcomes (death, AIDS, and serious non-AIDS events) among individuals who initiated ART immediately compared to those who delayed treatment. The benefits of early ART were consistent across different income levels and geographic regions. Similarly, the HPTN 052 trial demonstrated that early ART reduced the risk of HIV sexual transmission to uninfected partners by 93%. This trial involved 1,763 serodiscordant couples, mostly heterosexual, and showed that linked HIV transmissions were significantly lower in the early ART group. Importantly, no linked transmissions occurred when the HIV-positive partner’s viral load was stably suppressed by ART. The TEMPRANO trial provided moderate-quality evidence that initiating ART at a CD4 count above 500 cells/mm³ was not associated with an increased risk of severe adverse events. Observational data also suggested that earlier ART initiation improved ART uptake, linkage to care, and immune recovery, while reducing HIV transmission. However, some studies indicated a potential increase in laboratory adverse events, such as hepatic toxicity, though these did not lead to treatment discontinuation. For individuals with advanced HIV disease or CD4 counts below 350 cells/mm³, the benefits of ART initiation are well-established, including reduced mortality, slower disease progression, and lower incidence of opportunistic infections like tuberculosis. Late diagnosis and treatment initiation remain common, even in high-income settings, underscoring the need for earlier intervention. Expanding ART eligibility to all individuals living with HIV, regardless of CD4 count, is projected to avert millions of AIDS-related deaths and new infections by 2030. While the upfront costs of earlier ART initiation may increase, these are offset by reduced hospitalizations, improved productivity, and prevention of new infections. However, successful implementation requires high rates of HIV testing, treatment adherence, and retention in care. For pregnant and breastfeeding women, lifelong ART (Option B+) has become the preferred approach in most countries. This strategy improves maternal health, prevents mother-to-child transmission, and reduces horizontal transmission to uninfected sexual partners. Studies have shown that stopping ART postpartum leads to a decline in immune function and higher rates of loss to follow-up. The risks of lifelong ART, such as potential drug toxicity and adherence challenges, are similar to those faced by non-pregnant adults. In summary, the evidence strongly supports earlier and universal ART initiation for all individuals living with HIV, including pregnant and breastfeeding women, to improve health outcomes, reduce transmission, and simplify care delivery. However, successful implementation requires addressing structural barriers, ensuring equitable access, and maintaining high-quality care systems.
